question_en: An analyst gathers the following data: The bond has exactly 10 years until maturity and pays coupons annually. There are no other costs or benefits while holding the bond. A 1-year forward contract created with an initial value of zero most likely has an agreed-on price:
explanation_en: Futures price = Spot price + Cost of holding underlying − Benefits of holding underlying Derivative pricing is based on the no-arbitrage principle (ie, arbitrage-free pricing). This means that economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns. If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned. Futures price − Spot price = Cost of holding underlying − Benefits of holding underlying Benefits < costs Futures > spot Benefits > costs Futures < spot Benefits = costs Futures = spot Taking a long position in futures avoids the costs and forgoes any benefits of holding the underlying asset. For equivalent positions (eg, long stock = long stock futures + long a risk-free bond) to earn equal returns, futures and spot prices must differ by the net cost of holding the underlying asset until the expiration of the futures contract. When the benefits of holding the asset are greater than the costs of holding it, there is added value in holding the asset, so futures prices are below the spot price and not equal to or above it (Choices B and C). The net cost of holding a position in the underlying asset or commodity is called the cost of carry. The carry, as it is sometimes called, reflects the net of: costs—charges for storage, insurance, or financing the underlying position, versus benefits—income (ie, dividends or interest) or convenience yield from holding the underlying.

subtopic: 8.05 Pricing and Valuation of Forward Contracts and for an Underlying with Varying Maturities
question_en: The seller of a forward rate agreement (FRA) is most likely trying to:
explanation_en: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is a forward contract on an interest rate. In place of an underlying asset, FRAs have a reference interest rate (eg, 60-day LIBOR). A party that will borrow in the future can buy an FRA to hedge against an increase in interest rates, and potential lenders can sell an FRA to hedge against a decrease in interest rates. A loan is not originated through the FRA. Rather, a cash settlement occurs between the buyer (ie, long side) and the seller (ie, short side) at the FRA's expiration. The payment equals the difference between the current reference rate and the rate set in the FRA, discounted over the term of the hypothetical loan: Seller pays buyer if the reference rate is greater than the FRA rate. Buyer pays seller if the reference rate is less than the FRA rate. FRA buyers realize increasing gains as interest rates rise and incur increasing loses as rates fall, so a buyer's position is analogous to receiving a floating interest rate. Since the gains and losses accrue as the reference rate diverges from the FRA contract rate, the buyer's position is equivalent to borrowing at (ie, paying) a fixed rate equal to the FRA contract rate. (Choice B) Selling, not buying, an FRA is the equivalent of paying a floating interest rate and receiving a fixed interest rate. (Choice C) Paying a floating interest rate over one term and receiving a floating rate over a longer term creates a synthetic forward floating-rate note, not an FRA.

explanation_en: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is a derivative contract between two parties who have opposite expectations on how future interest rates will move. The long party ("buyer") believes that interest rates will increase, whereas the short party ("seller") believes they will decrease. The above diagram is a 30-day FRA, where the underlying is the interest rate for 90-day LIBOR on Day 30. Every FRA is initiated with a reference rate, which is the rate against which the actual 90-day LIBOR rate is compared when the agreement expires. If the actual 90-day rate on Day 30 is more than the reference rate, then the short party pays the long party. The long pays the short if the actual 90-day rate is less than the reference rate. For example, if the reference rate (ie, forward rate) is 6% and the 90-day LIBOR rate is 7% on Day 30, then the long party "wins." The short party pays the long party an amount based on the difference between the two rates (1%) multiplied by the notional principal amount, which was established when the FRA was initiated. (Choice A) The seller (ie, short party) of an FRA wants protection against a decline in interest rates, so a decline benefits the seller, not the buyer (ie, long party). (Choice B) If the actual interest rate when the FRA expires is the same as the FRA contract rate, neither party benefits.

question_en: A corporate borrower plans to close on a bank loan in 30 days, when the loan terms will be finalized. The interest rate on the loan is tied to 90- day LIBOR. Based on only this information, which of the following transactions most appropriately hedges the company's interest rate risk?
option_a: Long 30-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 90-day LIBOR
option_b: Long 90-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 90-day LIBOR
option_c: Long 120-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 90-day LIBOR
explanation_en: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is a forward contract on an interest rate. An FRA has a reference interest rate (eg, 180-day LIBOR) instead of an underlying asset. Buyers (ie, long parties) lock in the interest rate they will pay in a future period. Sellers (ie, short parties) lock in the interest rate they will receive in a future period. An FRA is sold to hedge the interest rate on a future investment (eg, when making a loan) or to speculate on falling interest rates and earn a profit if the reference rate at expiration is below the rate set in the agreement. Synthetic short FRAs are created by: buying longer maturity deposits (to receive an interest rate) and selling shorter maturity deposits (to pay an interest rate). In this case, buying (ie, going long) a 270-day deposit would fix the interest rate received for the term. Simultaneously selling (ie, going short) a 90-day deposit would require payment of a fixed interest rate, thereby offsetting the interest received for the first 90 days on the 270-day deposit. The combination of the two deposits results in a fixed rate of interest for a term of 180 days, starting 90 days in the future. That is the equivalent of selling a 90-day FRA on a 180-day rate. (Choice B) Going long a 180-day deposit and short a 90-day deposit is equivalent to selling a 90-day FRA on a 90-day interest rate. (Choice C) Unlike selling an FRA, going long a 90-day deposit and buying a 180-day deposit 90 days later does not lock in a future interest rate. The interest rate on the latter deposit is the market interest rate at its purchase.

subtopic: 8.06 Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
question_en: If interest rates are negatively correlated with futures prices, an increase in interest rate volatility most likely increases the prices of:
explanation_en: Forwards and futures are similar in that they are both firm commitments to purchase or sell an asset at a specified time in the future. However, futures have a daily settlement of gains or losses. In contrast, the gain or loss to a forward contract occurs at contract expiration. If futures prices and interest rates are negatively correlated, futures prices rise when rates are falling. This means that holders of long futures positions reinvest daily gains at lower interest rates. Conversely, as futures prices decline, the losses on long futures positions are financed at higher rates. As a result, long futures positions are at a disadvantage compared with long forward positions. Consequently, under these conditions, futures prices will be less than the prices of equivalent forwards, reflecting the relative disadvantage of futures to forwards. Moreover, volatility increases whatever differential exists between forward prices and futures prices, so in this case an increase in interest rate volatility means an increase in the price of forward contracts relative to the price of futures contracts (Choices A and C).

subtopic: 8.06 Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
question_en: All else equal, which of the following is most likely to cause futures and forward contract prices to differ? Differences in:
explanation_en: Futures vs. forward contracts Futures Forwards Trading venue Exchange-traded Over-the-counter Legal counterparty Exchange clearinghouse Contract counterparty Contract terms Standardized Negotiated (ie, nonstandardized) Gain/loss realization Daily settlement At expiration Forwards and futures with the same underlying asset and expiration may have different contract prices due to different cash flow patterns, reflecting the different timing of gain and loss realization: Forward contract gains and losses are realized at contract expiration. Futures contract gains and losses are realized daily. If futures prices are correlated with interest rates and if there is any interest rate volatility, the difference in the timing of gains and losses results in different futures and forward prices. Since futures contracts settle daily, their gains (losses) are reinvested (financed) sooner and more often than those of forward contracts, whose gains (losses) are reinvested (financed) only at expiration. This results in price differences. If interest rates are not correlated with futures or if interest rates are constant, futures and forward prices are equal. Since the prices of both types of contracts reflect cost of carry arbitrage pricing, neither liquidity nor counterparty credit risk affects the arbitrage- free futures or forward price (Choices A and B). Liquidity affects the size of the bid-ask spread; differences in counterparty credit risk affect the collateral that investors must provide to trade forwards but do not affect their prices.

subtopic: 8.06 Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
question_en: With regard to comparable futures and forward contracts, during times when futures prices are positively correlated with interest rates, futures are mostly likely priced:
explanation_en: Forwards and futures are similar, since both are firm commitments to purchase or sell an asset at a specified time in the future. Although there are several important differences between the two contracts, futures' daily settlement has the most impact on the discrepancy between futures and forward prices. Changes in futures' contract values are credited (or debited) daily to the contract holder's account. In contrast, the gain or loss on a forward contract occurs at contract expiration and is thus not available for reinvestment for months or years in the future. If interest rates are positively correlated with futures prices, when rates and futures prices rise, the long party can reinvest daily gains at higher rates. When rates and futures prices decline, losses can be financed by borrowing at lower rates. In either case, futures are more desirable than forwards to the long party, so futures are priced higher due to their relative advantage. Therefore, during periods when futures prices are positively correlated with interest rates, futures contracts are priced higher than comparable forward contracts. (Choice A) Futures are priced lower than forwards if interest rates are negatively correlated with futures prices. Daily settlement of gains and losses means that the long party to a futures contract reinvests gains at lower rates and faces higher rates for borrowing to finance losses. (Choice B) Futures and forwards are priced the same if there is no correlation between futures prices and interest rates.

subtopic: 8.07 Pricing and Valuation of Interest Rates and Other Swaps
question_en: Which of the following best replicates the cash flows of an interest rate swap? A series of:
explanation_en: Fixed-for-floating interest rate swaps are over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives in which counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. At each swap payment date: the floating payer owes cash to the fixed payer if the reference interest rate is greater than the swap's fixed rate, or the fixed payer owes cash to the floating payer if the reference interest rate is less than the swap's fixed rate. Swap cash flows are similar to forward rate agreements' (FRAs') cash flows (at expiration) since: the FRA seller (ie, short) pays the buyer (ie, long) if the reference interest rate is greater than the agreed rate, and the FRA buyer (ie, long) pays the seller (ie, short) if the reference rate is less than the agreed rate. Given this similarity, the swap's cash flows can be replicated by a portfolio of FRAs with expirations matching each swap payment date, all having agreed interest rates equal to the swap's fixed rate. (Choice A) Unlike FRAs, futures are exchange-traded derivatives that generate daily cash flows since they are marked to market every trading session. Although a portfolio of interest rate futures could create similar market exposure to that of an interest rate swap, a portfolio of futures could not replicate a swap's cash flows. (Choice B) Holders of interest rate calls never incur negative cash flows at expiration. Holders receive either the in-the-money call value in cash or nothing. In contrast, swaps may have positive or negative cash flows on the payment dates.

question_en: A swap contract is priced so that it has a value of zero at initiation. If the value of the underlying changes during the life of a swap contract, the most likely impact is that:
option_a: only the price of the swap changes.
option_b: only the value of the swap changes.
option_c: both the value and price of the swap change.
explanation_en: Swaps: pricing vs. valuation Definition Method Time horizon Setting terms so contract has an Set fixed rate so present values of payments from Full length of contract from Pricing initial value of zero counterparties are equal initiation Determining contract's value after Determine difference between present values of Remaining life of contract from Valuation initiation fixed and floating payments valuation date Although the terms pricing and valuation are used interchangeably in some contexts, they have distinct meanings when used in regard to swaps. Swap pricing refers to setting contract terms at initiation, and value refers to determining the value of a swap after initiation. Both counterparties are paying and receiving, so the value of the swap is simply the difference in the present value of the future cash flow streams. Most swaps are priced to have an initial value of zero since both sides enter into the swap to exchange cash flows of equivalent value. The swap's value at any time after initiation is affected by changes in market conditions and by the fluctuating value of the underlying. As these changes and fluctuations occur, the values of the cash flow streams change for each counterparty. The difference is reflected in the swap's value, which is the net difference in the present values of its cash flows (Choices A and C).

question_en: Initiating a fixed-for-floating swap at terms that result in the contract having an initial value of zero is most likely referred to as swap:
explanation_en: Swaps: pricing vs. valuation Definition Method Time horizon Setting terms so contract has an Set fixed rate so present values of payments from Full length of contract from Pricing initial value of zero counterparties are equal initiation Determining contract's value after Determine difference between present values of Remaining life of contract from Valuation initiation fixed and floating payments valuation date A fixed-for-floating interest rate swap is a contract in which the counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. Though pricing and valuation are used interchangeably in some contexts, the terms have distinct meanings when used in connection with swaps. Swap pricing refers to setting the contract terms so that no payment is required of either counterparty at initiation. The fixed rate is established so that the present value of fixed swap payments equals the present value of the floating payments, resulting in a contract with an initial value of zero. That process involves replicating the swap with a series of forward contracts that hedges (ie, locks in) the amounts due for the series of floating payments. The fixed payment coupon rate is a blended average of the rates locked in by the replicating strategy (ie, forward contracts). (Choice B) Swap valuation refers to determining a swap's value after initiation to capture the impact of the passage of time and changing market conditions. (Choice C) Collateralization is the means of managing counterparty credit risk of over-the-counter derivatives, including swaps. Collateral requirements are based on a swap counterparty's financial condition and are not a consideration when pricing swaps.

option_a: determining the amount of cash owed on a swap payment date.
option_b: establishing the amount payable for early termination of a swap.
option_c: setting the contract terms so the swap has an initial value of zero.

The swap's floating payment stream can be replicated as a portfolio of forward contracts that hedge the amounts due for the series of floating payments. The periodic fixed payment is priced or set so it equates the present value of the fixed and floating payment streams at initiation. A swap's value is the difference between the present values of the fixed and floating payment streams remaining until contract expiration.

question_en: A one-year fixed-for-floating swap contract that specifies quarterly payment dates is most similar to a:
option_a: one-year floating-rate note with quarterly coupon payments.
option_b: portfolio of cash-settled long call options expiring in 3, 6, 9, and 12 months.
option_c: portfolio of cash-settled forward contracts expiring in 3, 6, 9, and 12 months.
explanation_en: A fixed-for-floating interest rate swap is a contract in which the counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. As is the case at swap payment dates, the cash flows at the forwards' expirations can be positive or negative. At each expiration date for the forward contract portfolio: the seller (ie, short) pays the buyer (ie, long) if the reference asset's value is greater than the agreed price, or the buyer (ie, long) pays the seller (ie, short) if the reference asset's value is less than the agreed price. For both the swap and the portfolio of forwards the size of the cash payment increases the greater the difference between the reference asset's value and the agreed price or fixed swap payment. (Choice A) The cash flows (ie, coupon payments) from holding floating-rate notes (FRNs) are always positive, unlike swaps, for which the cash flows on the payment dates could be positive or negative. question_en: Assuming a forward market in contango, a fixed-for-floating swap with an initial value of zero is most likely equivalent to a series of forward contracts with:
option_a: different agreed-on prices having a net initial value of zero.
option_b: the same agreed-on price having a net initial value of zero.
option_c: the same agreed-on price, each having an initial value of zero.
explanation_en: A fixed-for-floating swap is a contract in which the counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. To achieve an initial contract value of zero, the fixed swap payments are set so that their present value equals the present value of the floating payments. The process involves replicating the swap cash flows. The fixed swap payments can be viewed as a blended average of the floating payments, locked in by the replicating strategy of a forward contract. When a market is in contango, forward contracts with different expirations must have different agreed-on prices to be at market (ie, have initial values of zero). Therefore, for a market in contango a series of forward contracts with the same agreed-on price (ie, fixed swap payments) have different values. Some of the fixed swap payments have negative values (ie, fixed payment > forward price) and others have positive values (ie, fixed payment < forward price). The fixed swap payments are set so that their net value is zero when the swap is initiated. (Choice A) The series of fixed swap payments is equivalent to a series of forward contracts that have the same agreed-on price, not different agreed-on prices. (Choice C) When a market is in contango, forward contracts in a series with the same agreed-on price cannot all have an initial value of zero.

question_en: A fixed-for-floating interest rate swap has two years until expiration. The counterparties have just completed the cash settlement for a scheduled payment date two years prior to contract expiration. Which of the following best describes the value of the swap?
option_b: The net present value of the cash flows until contract expiration
option_c: The net present value of the cash flows due at the next payment date
explanation_en: Swaps: pricing vs. valuation Definition Method Time horizon Setting terms so contract has an Set fixed rate so present values of payments from Full length of contract from Pricing initial value of zero counterparties are equal initiation Determining contract's value after Determine difference between present values of Remaining life of contract from Valuation initiation fixed and floating payments valuation date Fixed-for-floating interest rate swaps require counterparties to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. A swap's value at any time prior to expiration is the difference between the present value of the remaining fixed payments and the present value of the remaining floating payments. Swaps are usually structured to have an initial value of zero. Fixed-for-floating interest rate swaps achieve this result when the coupon rate for the fixed payments is set so that the present values of the fixed cash flow series and the floating cash flow series are equal. However, interest rates change over time, so the value of a swap changes and does not reset to zero (Choice A). (Choice C) The value of a swap is equal to the net present value of the cash flows due at the next payment date only during the payment period ending at expiration. Since swaps have periodic payment dates (eg, semiannual), a swap with two years until expiration is not entering the final payment period.

question_en: At contract initiation, the value of a fixed-for-floating swap is most likely:
option_c: unable to be determined, since future interest rates are unknown.
explanation_en: A fixed-for-floating swap is an agreement in which two parties (the swap buyer and swap seller) exchange cash flows at regular intervals, such as every six months, over a specified period, such as two years. On each payment date, the swap buyer pays an amount based on a fixed interest rate, and the seller pays an amount based on a variable (ie, "floating") interest rate. Both payments are calculated using notional principal. At any time, the value of the swap to either party is the present value of the difference between the amount that the party expects to pay and the amount it expects to receive. However, the value of a swap is different than its price. The price is the fixed interest rate, which is also known as the swap rate (Choice B). Changes in the swap's value depend on changes in the variable rate during its life. Since neither party will enter into the agreement if it starts at a disadvantage, the swap's value must be the same for both parties at initiation. This requirement is satisfied only if the value at initiation is zero, when neither party has an advantage or a disadvantage. (Choice C) At initiation, the swap's floating payments are based on expected future variable rates, so certainty as to future rates is not needed to value the swap. If the expected variable rates are known, the swap rate can be set so that the value at initiation is zero.

question_en: An increase in the risk-free interest rate is most likely to cause the arbitrage-free value of European equity put option to:
explanation_en: The no-arbitrage value of a European equity put option is determined by the market price of the underlying stock and an otherwise equivalent (ie, same underlying equity, strike price, and time to expiry) European call. Risk-free interest rates affect option values through their impact on the present value of the strike price. All else equal, the value of a European equity put decreases when the risk-free rate increases (Choices B and C). This result for European puts follows from the: Put owner receiving the strike price if the option is exercised at expiration, and Higher interest rates reducing the present value of the money received, should the option be exercised.
